intro: The web threat model and defences that come up in frontend and full-stack interviews.

entries.short: Untrusted data runs as script in your origin.
entries.medium: Stored persists the payload, reflected bounces it off a request, DOM happens when client code writes untrusted data into a sink. Prevent with output encoding for the context, avoid innerHTML and raw-HTML escape hatches, and sanitize HTML with a library like DOMPurify.
entries.detail: CSP and HttpOnly reduce the impact but do not replace encoding. Framework auto-escaping is bypassed the moment you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

entries.short: Another site makes the browser send an authenticated request.
entries.medium: Cookies are attached automatically, so the request looks authenticated. Defend with SameSite cookies, a CSRF token another origin cannot read, Fetch Metadata or origin checks, and no side effects on GET.
entries.detail: HttpOnly does not prevent CSRF: the browser still sends the cookie. Bearer tokens in a header from memory largely avoid the classic attack.

entries.short: Script cannot read responses from another origin.
entries.medium: An origin is scheme, host and port. The policy restricts reading, not sending. CORS is the server granting specific origins permission to read, via response headers.
entries.detail: It is a browser rule. Servers and scripts are not bound by it, which is why the server must still authorize every request.

entries.short: Response headers that allow specific origins to read.
entries.medium: Non-simple requests trigger a preflight OPTIONS. Credentialed requests require Access-Control-Allow-Credentials and an exact origin, never the wildcard. CORS is not authentication or authorization.
entries.detail: Reflecting any Origin is equivalent to allowing all. Add Vary: Origin when the response depends on the request origin.

entries.short: HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite each stop a different thing.
entries.medium: HttpOnly hides the cookie from script, blunting token theft by XSS. Secure sends it only over HTTPS. SameSite=Lax blocks most cross-site POSTs, and Strict is stronger but breaks inbound navigations.
entries.detail: SameSite=None requires Secure. None of these stop a server that fails to authorize, and HttpOnly does not stop CSRF.

entries.short: localStorage is XSS-readable; HttpOnly cookies need CSRF defence.
entries.medium: localStorage is the easiest and the weakest, since any XSS reads it. HttpOnly cookies resist theft but are sent automatically. A common balance is a short-lived access token in memory plus a refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.
entries.detail: Whichever you pick, keep access tokens short-lived, rotate refresh tokens, and remember storage never fixes broken authorization.

entries.short: A header that allow-lists where content may load from.
entries.medium: script-src is the key directive. Disallowing inline scripts and using a per-response nonce blocks injected scripts. Deploy in Report-Only mode first to find what would break.
entries.detail: It is defence in depth, not a replacement for output encoding. unsafe-inline or a broad allow-list provides little protection.

entries.short: Untrusted input concatenated into a query becomes code.
entries.medium: Parameterised queries send the query and the values separately, so a value can never change the structure. Use them everywhere, including raw ORM escape hatches.
entries.detail: Least-privilege database users limit the blast radius if something slips through.

entries.short: Your page is framed and overlaid to hijack clicks.
entries.medium: Block framing with CSP frame-ancestors 'none' or 'self'. X-Frame-Options is the older header and is largely superseded by frame-ancestors.
entries.detail: For embeds you must allow, sandbox the iframe and validate postMessage origins rather than trusting the message data.

entries.short: A small set of headers that close common gaps.
entries.medium: Content-Security-Policy restricts sources. Strict-Transport-Security forces HTTPS. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops MIME sniffing. Referrer-Policy limits leakage. frame-ancestors prevents framing.
entries.detail: Set them at the edge or in the server framework so they apply to every response, not just some routes.

entries.short: Anything shipped to the browser is public.
entries.medium: Bundled API keys, tokens and credentials are readable by anyone. Keep secrets on the server and proxy calls that need them. Use short-lived, scoped tokens for third-party services.
entries.detail: Environment variables prefixed for client exposure are compiled into the bundle, so treat them as public.

entries.short: Your dependencies are part of your attack surface.
entries.medium: Lockfiles, automated audits, and Subresource Integrity hashes for third-party scripts reduce risk. Pin versions and review what you install.
entries.detail: A compromised transitive dependency can run in your build or your page, so least-install and audit are real controls.

entries.short: Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may do.
entries.medium: Never trust the client for authorization. Check ownership and role on the server for every request, including object-level checks so a user cannot read another user's record by changing an id.
entries.detail: Broken object-level authorization is one of the most common real-world API vulnerabilities, and CORS does nothing to prevent it.
